systemPrompt:
You are an assistant helping a developer with their CircleCI projects. Answer the user's question using only the tools provided to you. Ground every claim in data you actually retrieved; if you cannot retrieve something, say so. Do not change anything in the project beyond what the user explicitly asks for. Finish with a clear, direct answer to the question.

The current directory is a checkout of the CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli repository. You can inspect its files with the read-only list_files and read_file tools.

This server exposes CircleCI: the CI pipelines an org runs, the deploys those
pipelines produce, and the config, orbs, functions and usage data around them. Every tool
acts as the authenticated user and sees only what that user can see.

Ids are UUIDs and are not interchangeable — a run id, a workflow id and a job
id are distinct, and a tool handed the wrong kind fails rather than guessing.
Nothing accepts a job number or a CircleCI web URL. Projects and orgs are the
exception: they take either a slug ("gh/org/repo", "gh/org") or a UUID.

SKILLS. This server ships written playbooks for the work that takes several
of the tools below — the orderings, the costs and the usual mistakes, which
no single tool description can carry:

    list_skills  the catalog: what each playbook covers, and its references
    get_skill    one playbook, or one of its bundled references

Before working through the tools below, call list_skills once and load any
skill whose description covers the work, together with the related skills it
names. It takes no arguments and returns the whole catalog, so that one call
is the entire search. If nothing clearly fits, load nothing and work from the
tool descriptions. One pass serves a whole session: having listed once, do not
list again. The one exception is a failed run you hold the id of: call
get_run_failure_report first, and look for a skill only if it leaves the
cause open.

A skill earns its call at the start of a piece of work, not after one has gone
wrong. The same guides are readable as resources under circleci://skills/ for
clients that browse resources rather than call tools.

PIPELINES. The tools form a chain, each level's id feeding the next:

    list_runs -> get_run -> list_run_workflows -> get_workflow -> list_workflow_jobs -> get_job

Enter at list_runs; it is the only one of these that takes a project rather
than a UUID. With no project named, mine=true lists the user's own runs across
every project. Skip levels whenever you already hold an id — get_run is
pointless if you have the run id and want its workflows. trigger_run starts a
new run and returns its id, which enters the chain at get_run.

If you hold a run id and want to know why it failed, call
get_run_failure_report first; you do not need list_skills or any tool in the
chain before it. It walks the chain in one call and returns the failed steps
with their exit codes and condensed output, plus the job id, execution and step
num the tools below take; on a very wide run it says what it left out. Reach
for those tools only for what the report leaves open.

For the files a run stored — a coverage report, test results, a build
output — call list_run_artifacts with the run id rather than walking the chain
and calling list_job_artifacts once per job: it reads every job's artifacts in
one call, and path narrows them to the ones wanted. For the latest successful
run, take the id from list_runs with status "success" and limit 1.

DIAGNOSING A JOB. Five tools take a job id and answer different questions.
Which you pick matters more than the order:

    get_job                 which step failed and its exit code, or why it never ran
    list_job_tests          which tests failed
    get_job_logs            what a step printed
    get_job_resource_usage  whether it ran out of CPU or memory
    list_job_artifacts      the files it persisted, with download URLs

Start with get_job — it is cheap and names the failed step — unless
get_run_failure_report already did. If that step ran
tests, go to list_job_tests, which is far cheaper than logs and already
filtered to failures. Reach for get_job_logs only when you need the output
itself; it is the most expensive tool here, so keep tail_lines small. If a job
died with nothing in its logs, check get_job_resource_usage for an OOM.

FLAKY TESTS. list_flaky_tests takes a project, not a job, and answers "which
tests are flaky?" in one call: tests that failed and then passed within the
same pipeline, counted across the project's runs, most-flaked first. Reach for
it instead of walking runs and jobs to compare outcomes, and to check whether
a test that just failed is a known flake before treating it as a regression.

DEPLOYS are a separate subsystem, keyed on projects and orgs rather than on
pipeline ids, and reachable without touching a run:

    list_deployments                what was deployed — to a project, or across an org
    list_deploy_components          a project's deployable units
    list_deploy_environments        an org's release targets (production, staging)
    list_deploy_component_versions  a component's version history
    get_deploy_component            one component by id
    get_deploy_environment          one environment by id

For "what is live" or "when did X ship", use list_deployments — pass project for
a single project or org for everything in the org. The two get_ tools resolve an
id you already hold back to its name; the list tools already return names, so reach
for them only when an id arrived from somewhere else.

CONFIG, ORBS AND FUNCTIONS need no CircleCI resource at all; they work on YAML
you hold:

    validate_config  compile a config and report its errors
    get_orb          an orb's published versions — whether a pin is stale
    get_orb_source   an orb's YAML — how to call its jobs and commands
    list_functions   every published function, with its versions
    get_function     one function's arguments, versions, and the config that uses it

Read an orb's source before writing config against it, and compile a config
before pushing it rather than after. To add a function, take the declaration
and step get_function returns and edit the config yourself: nothing here
writes to it.

When writing a new config, or adding a setup or test step to one, call
list_functions first and use the matching function; write a run: step
only when none fits. Orbs remain supported for existing pipelines, so do
not move a working orb-based config to functions unless the user asks.

WRITES. trigger_run is additive: it starts a new run of a project's branch or tag.
rerun_workflow is additive: it creates a new workflow. cancel_workflow
stops running work. rollback_deploy_component redeploys production software.
Confirm with the user before calling any of them unless they asked for it
directly — and for a rollback, confirm the component, the environment and both
versions rather than just the intent.

Also: get_me for the authenticated user's identity and ids, and
download_usage_data for an org's billing CSVs (asynchronous — start an export,
then poll it).

FEEDBACK. send_feedback reports a problem with this server to CircleCI — an
error that looks like CircleCI's fault, a capability that is missing, or a
tool that misled you. Errors that look like CircleCI's fault end by pointing
to it. Report once per distinct problem, saying what you were trying to do and
what happened. It changes nothing in CircleCI, so unlike the writes above it
needs no confirmation. Report functions too: when you write a run: step
because no function does the job, or because one falls short, send it with
type and function.

When a tool errors, read the message before retrying. Most errors here say
what was wrong — the wrong kind of id, a missing project, an execution index
out of range — and the same arguments will fail the same way.

Target CircleCI project: gh/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli (organization: gh/CircleCI-Public).

Skill track-deploys (6490 bytes of markdown)
{"content":"# Track what shipped

Deploys are a separate subsystem from pipelines. They are keyed on projects and
orgs rather than on run, workflow or job ids, so none of this needs a run — and
a deploy carries the ids of the pipeline that produced it, which is the bridge
back the other way.

## 1. Start at the deployments list

    list_deployments {project: "gh/org/repo", limit: 20}

This needs only a project, and it answers most of what gets asked: what was
last deployed, when a version went out, whether the last deploy succeeded.
Reach for it before walking components and environments, which cost several
calls to arrive at the same place.

Each deployment carries:

| Field | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| `component_name`, `version` | What shipped |
| `status` | Whether it finished, and how |
| `created_at`, `ended_at` | When it started and stopped. `ended_at` absent means it is still going. |
| `is_rollback` | Whether this deploy was itself a rollback — so a version going backwards in the list is explained rather than mysterious |
| `pipeline_id`, `workflow_id` | The CI run behind it |
| `component_id` | Feeds the component tools below |

Deployments come newest-first, capped by `limit` (default 20). `truncated`
reports that more exist; raise `limit` rather than paging.

**What the list does not carry is the environment.** There is no environment id
on a deployment, so "what is live in production" is not answerable from this
call alone when a component deploys to more than one place — use
`list_deploy_component_versions` with an `environment` filter for that.

## 2. Is a deploy the cause?

The common question. Two checks, and the order matters:

1. **Timing.** Compare the deployment's `created_at` and `ended_at` against
   when the symptom started. A deploy that *finished after* the symptom began
   did not cause it. A deploy still in flight — no `ended_at` — may be causing
   it right now, and may be half-applied.
2. **Whether it is even a candidate.** A deployment with a failed `status` may
   have left the environment in a mixed state, which is a different problem
   from a bad version being live. Read `status` before blaming `version`.

Then say which it is. Timing that lines up is a correlation, and these tools
cannot see the deployed software's behaviour — they know versions and
timestamps, nothing about what the code does. Say "this deploy is the only
change in the window" rather than "this deploy caused it", unless something
else establishes the cause.

**Across several projects**, there is no org-wide deployments tool: call
`list_deployments` once per candidate project. You have to name the candidates
— the server has no way to list the projects that deployed recently — so ask
which services are in scope rather than guessing at slugs.

To cross into CI, take the deployment's `workflow_id` and go to
`list_workflow_jobs`; the `debug-failing-run` skill takes it from there.

## 3. Detail, when the list is not enough

Three tools, each needing the id above it:

    list_deploy_components {project}                    a project's deployable units
    list_deploy_component_versions {component, environment?}   a component's release history
    list_deploy_environments {org}                      an org's targets (production, staging)

`list_deploy_component_versions` is the one that answers "what is live in
production": filter it with the `environment` uuid from
`list_deploy_environments`, and read the newest entry. Versions are newest-first
and capped at 20 by default, and an actively deployed component can have far
more, so narrow by environment before raising `limit`.

`get_deploy_component` and `get_deploy_environment` only resolve an id you
already hold back to its name. The list tools return names already, so reach
for these two only when an id arrived from somewhere else — a rollback plan
someone else wrote, a log line, an earlier answer.

Note the asymmetry: **components belong to a project, environments belong to an
org.** Passing a project where an org is wanted is the usual mistake here.

## 4. Rolling back

`rollback_deploy_component` redeploys production software. Treat it as a plan to
be approved, not a call to make: gather everything, state the plan, and wait.

**Confirm with the user before calling it** unless they asked for a rollback
directly — and even then, state the component, the environment, and both
versions, and get agreement on those specifics.

Five required arguments, all of which must be *read* rather than assumed:

| Argument | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| `project` | The slug or UUID you already have |
| `component` | `list_deploy_components` |
| `environment` | `list_deploy_environments` (org-scoped) |
| `current_version` | `list_deployments` or `list_deploy_component_versions` |
| `target_version` | `list_deploy_component_versions` |

`current_version` is a safety interlock, not a formality: the rollback is
refused unless it really is the deployed version. That refusal is the API
catching you working from a stale picture — re-read the deployments rather than
trying other values.

Pass the user's stated reason as `reason`. It is recorded in the audit log, and
a rollback with no reason is a thing someone will have to reconstruct later.

**A successful call means the rollback started, not that the target version is
live.** `rollback_type` says how it is being carried out — a rollback pipeline
run, or a release-agent command — and `id` is that run or command. Follow it to
confirm the rollback landed, and say which of the two you are looking at.

`checkout_ref`, `config_ref` and `parameters` steer a rollback *pipeline* and
are silently ignored when the project has no rollback pipeline configured, so
do not reach for them to fix a rollback that is not working. `namespace` scopes
the component within the environment and defaults to `default`.

See `references/rollback.md` for the preflight sequence and the failure modes
worth recognising.

## Report the state, not the tour

Name what is live, when it shipped, and — if a rollback is on the table — the
exact plan: this component, in this environment, from this version to that one.
For an incident question, give the deploy window against the symptom window and
say plainly whether it is a candidate or ruled out.

## Reference

- `references/rollback.md` — the preflight sequence before a rollback call,
  what each failure means, and how to confirm one landed.

**This week (Mon 5 Oct – Tue 6 Oct 2026, UTC)**

| Deployed (UTC) | Version | Commit / PR | How the pipeline started | User ID on the pipeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 6, 08:56 | `1.0.52170-e0dfe1e` | `e0dfe1e`, PR #1877 (`st/shared-pipeline-config-flag`) | **API call** on `main` | `69f6066c-bc60-40c0-b945-e746697220bb` |

| Oct 5, 14:59 | `1.0.52016-a385f0b` | `a385f0b`, PR #1856 (`st/fn-8-update`) | Push to `main` (GitHub webhook) | `b615b46c-c6fe-43c8-998e-f88dff349780` |

**Who triggered them**
- **All three commits are by Samba siva Tiyyagura (`stiyyagura0901`).** That's who wrote the code. It doesn't prove who started each deploy.
- **The two Oct 5 deploys** started automatically when PRs #1856 and #1877 were merged to `main`. Both came from the same CircleCI user ID.
- **The Oct 6 deploy** was a second build of the same commit as the Oct 5 15:45 deploy. Someone started it with an API call, and it's under a different user ID. I can't tell why they rebuilt it.
- **I can't turn these user IDs into names.** No tool here looks up users. Neither ID is you (`alexandrahsu-eng`), and I didn't check them against GitHub.

**Caveats**
- **"Production":** The org's deploy environments include `default`, `orbs-dev` and several ECS/EKS test clusters, but nothing called production. Deployment records don't say which environment they went to. All three versions above do show up under the `default` environment, so I've treated that as the release target. Tell me if production means something else for you.
- **"This week":** I don't have today's date. I took the week to start on Monday, Oct 5, because Oct 6 is the newest deployment. Counting from Thursday, Oct 1 instead adds six more successful deploys: Oct 2 at 14:00, 13:01 and 11:38, and Oct 1 at 22:15, 21:30 and 10:42 (UTC). Their triggers are a quick lookup if you want them.
